title: Nationalism: Unification of Italy and Germany

cards.b: The nationalism that Europe’s revolutions spread made new states in 1861 and 1871. UPSC asks for the role of leaders and methods, and for comparisons.

The Congress of Vienna (1815) split Italy into states under Austria and the Bourbons; Germany became a 39-state German Confederation led by Austria. Liberal and national movements rose: revolutions of 1830 and 1848 (the “spring of nations”). They mostly failed, but the idea of a nation had taken root.

Giuseppe Mazzini founded the Carbonari-era Young Italy (1831) and wanted a republic. Cavour, prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia under King Victor Emmanuel II, wanted a monarchy through diplomacy. Garibaldi led the Red Shirts. Austria was the main enemy. The Risorgimento (resurgence) was both ideas and war.

• 1859: Cavour allied with Napoleon III against Austria (Plombières, 1858); Lombardy gained.
  • 1860: Garibaldi’s thousand Red Shirts took Sicily and Naples.
  • 1861: Kingdom of Italy proclaimed; Victor Emmanuel II king.
  • 1866: Venetia (after the Austro-Prussian war).
  • 1870: Rome taken when French troops withdrew.

Zollverein (1834): a customs union led by Prussia. Bismarck (minister-president from 1862): “blood and iron”, Realpolitik. Wars: against Denmark (1864; Schleswig-Holstein), Austria (1866, Sadowa/Königgrätz; the North German Confederation), France (1870 to 71, Sedan). On 18 January 1871 William I was proclaimed German emperor at Versailles.

A federal empire with a strong Prussian king, a Reichstag elected by universal male suffrage and a chancellor who answered to the emperor. Bismarck’s later policy: Kulturkampf against Catholics, anti-socialist laws and welfare, alliance system (Three Emperors’ League, Triple Alliance 1882), Berlin Congress (1878) and conference (1884 to 85). He was dismissed by William II in 1890.

Italy was made by diplomacy and foreign help more than people’s rising; Germany by Prussian power. A. J. P. Taylor (The Struggle for Mastery in Europe) saw Bismarck as an opportunist. Historians such as Hans-Ulrich Wehler see “top-down” unification. Liberals thought unity meant freedom; instead it meant strong states.

Indian leaders in the 1900s drew on Mazzini; Savarkar translated Mazzini’s writings; Tilak and the Extremists admired Garibaldi. India’s integration of princely states in 1947 (Patel as the “Bismarck of India”) is often compared. Debates on nationalism, federalism and diversity in a union echo the German model.

• “Compare the unification of Italy and Germany.” Table: leaders, methods, states, outcome.
  • “Role of Bismarck.”
  • Prelims tip: Zollverein 1834; Italy 1861; Rome 1870; Sedan 1870; German Empire proclaimed 1871 at Versailles.
